title: Moles and Molar Mass
overview: A mole connects laboratory-scale mass with numbers of microscopic particles. Use the identity of the substance to decide whether you are counting atoms, molecules or formula units before choosing a conversion factor.

keyConcepts.title: Molar mass
keyConcepts.text: Add the atomic masses indicated by the chemical formula. Molar mass has units of grams per mole; subscripts affect this sum.

keyConcepts.title: Conversions
keyConcepts.text: Use n = m/M and N = nNₐ, with Nₐ approximately 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole. Cancel units at every step.

keyConcepts.title: Particle identity
keyConcepts.text: A mole of molecules is not necessarily a mole of atoms. Multiply by the relevant subscript when counting atoms within a compound.

example.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in 8.80 g of CO₂? Use M(CO₂) = 44.0 g/mol.
steps: Convert mass: 8.80/44.0 = 0.200 mol CO₂.
Each molecule contains two oxygen atoms: 0.200 × 2 = 0.400 mol O atoms.
example.conclusion: Multiply by Nₐ: 0.400 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.41 × 10²³ oxygen atoms, to three significant figures.

misconception: Equal mole amounts contain equal numbers of the specified entities, not equal masses. Compare formulas and molar masses before making a mass claim.
apTip: Write the particle name next to each numerical answer. This prevents confusing total atoms with molecules when interpreting a particulate diagram.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.1; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Recomputed mass-to-mole conversion and oxygen multiplicity separately. Avogadro factor counts atoms after, not before, the factor of two.

title: Mass Spectra of Elements
overview: A mass spectrum identifies isotopes through their mass-to-charge ratios and relative abundances. For the singly charged atomic ions typically used in introductory isotope problems, peak positions approximate isotope masses rather than average atomic mass.

keyConcepts.title: Isotopes
keyConcepts.text: Isotopes of one element share a proton count but differ in neutron count. Their chemical identities are therefore the same despite different masses.

keyConcepts.title: Peak abundance
keyConcepts.text: Relative peak heights or areas represent isotope abundance under the stated measurement convention. Convert percentages to fractions and normalize ratios when needed.

keyConcepts.title: Weighted average
keyConcepts.text: Calculate average atomic mass by multiplying each isotope mass by its fractional abundance, then adding the contributions. The result lies between the isotope masses.

example.prompt: A hypothetical element has isotopes of mass 62.0 u and 64.0 u at abundances of 75.0% and 25.0%. Find its average atomic mass.
steps: Use fractions 0.750 and 0.250, whose sum is one.
example.conclusion: The weighted mean is 62.5 u, closer to the more abundant lighter isotope.

misconception: The tallest peak is the most abundant isotope, not automatically the average mass. A mean need not coincide with an actual isotope peak.
apTip: Check whether the problem specifies atomic ions or molecular fragments before assigning peaks. Explain averages using abundance as well as mass.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.2; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Weighted contributions independently recomputed; hypothetical masses avoid confusing mass number with measured isotope mass.

title: Elemental Composition of Pure Substances
overview: A pure compound has a fixed ratio of its constituent elements. Elemental mass data can reveal an empirical formula, while a separate molar-mass measurement can determine the molecular formula.

keyConcepts.title: Mass fractions
keyConcepts.text: Divide an element’s mass contribution in one mole by the compound’s molar mass. Multiply by 100 to express mass percent.

keyConcepts.title: Empirical formula
keyConcepts.text: Convert each element’s mass to moles, divide by the smallest mole amount, then obtain whole-number ratios. Do not compare gram ratios directly.

keyConcepts.title: Molecular formula
keyConcepts.text: Divide molecular molar mass by empirical-formula molar mass. This whole-number factor multiplies every empirical-formula subscript.

example.prompt: A pure carbon–hydrogen compound is 80.0% carbon and 20.0% hydrogen by mass. Use C = 12.0 and H = 1.00 g/mol; its molar mass is 30.0 g/mol.
steps: For a 100 g sample, n(C) = 80.0/12.0 = 6.67 mol and n(H) = 20.0 mol.
Divide both by 6.67: the ratio is approximately 1:3, so the empirical formula is CH₃.
example.conclusion: CH₃ has mass 15.0 g/mol. The factor 30.0/15.0 = 2 gives the molecular formula C₂H₆.

misconception: An empirical formula reports the simplest whole-number ratio; it need not represent an individual molecule.
apTip: Use unrounded intermediate mole amounts when establishing ratios. Multiply all ratios together if a simple fraction remains.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.3; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Rechecked 80/12 and H:C = 3; empirical mass 15 and molecular factor 2 yield C2H6, with 24/30 = 80% carbon.

title: Composition of Mixtures
overview: A mixture contains substances physically combined in proportions that can vary. Its overall composition reflects the amounts of its components, rather than a single chemical formula describing every particle.

keyConcepts.title: Mixture versus compound
keyConcepts.text: A pure compound has a fixed composition and chemically bonded elements. A mixture can contain elements or compounds without forming a new chemical substance.

keyConcepts.title: Mass accounting
keyConcepts.text: Component masses add to the total mass in a closed preparation. Mass fraction equals component mass divided by total mixture mass.

keyConcepts.title: Separation evidence
keyConcepts.text: Physical methods exploit properties such as solubility, volatility or particle size. Choose a method that separates the actual components without assuming a chemical reaction.

example.prompt: A dry mixture contains 6.00 g NaCl and 4.00 g sand. Water dissolves the salt but not the sand. How much of the original mixture is NaCl by mass?
steps: The initial total is 6.00 + 4.00 = 10.00 g.
The salt mass fraction is 6.00/10.00 = 0.600, or 60.0%.
example.conclusion: Dissolving, filtering off sand and evaporating the water can recover salt; the added water is not part of the original dry-mixture mass.

misconception: A homogeneous appearance does not prove purity: a salt solution is uniform but contains multiple substances.
apTip: Identify exactly which sample the denominator describes. Distinguish the original mixture from a later solution containing added solvent.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.4; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Closed initial mass balance and fraction checked; filtration removes insoluble sand while dissolved salt passes with water.

title: Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration
overview: An electron configuration describes how electrons occupy atomic energy levels and subshells. It connects atomic structure to periodic position and helps explain which electrons are removed when ions form.

keyConcepts.title: Subshell occupancy
keyConcepts.text: An s subshell holds up to two electrons and a p subshell up to six. Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

keyConcepts.title: Ground-state arrangement
keyConcepts.text: Electrons occupy lower-energy available orbitals first. Within equal-energy orbitals, they occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing.

keyConcepts.title: Ion formation
keyConcepts.text: Count electrons using atomic number and charge. For main-group cations, remove electrons from the outer occupied principal level; do not remove core electrons first.

example.prompt: Write the ground-state configurations of Mg and Mg²⁺, given atomic number 12.
steps: Neutral Mg has twelve electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s². The exponents sum to 12.
Mg²⁺ has lost two electrons from the outer 3s subshell, leaving ten electrons.
example.conclusion: The ion is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, or [Ne]. Its nucleus still contains twelve protons.

misconception: A positive ion has fewer electrons than its neutral atom, not fewer protons. Changing proton count would change the element.
apTip: Check both the total electron count and the occupied outer level. Relate configuration to charge rather than memorizing a symbol alone.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.5; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Configuration totals independently counted: 2+2+6+2=12; cation loses 3s electrons, with protons unchanged.

title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy
overview: Photoelectron spectroscopy measures the energy needed to eject electrons from occupied atomic subshells. Peak positions show binding energies, while relative peak intensities help identify the numbers of electrons represented.

keyConcepts.title: Binding energy
keyConcepts.text: A tightly attracted core electron generally has a larger binding energy than an outer electron. Read the axis direction because spectra may place larger energies on either side.

keyConcepts.title: Peak occupancy
keyConcepts.text: Under the problem’s stated intensity model, relative peak area reflects electron population. Use both position and relative intensity to assign subshells.

keyConcepts.title: Comparing atoms
keyConcepts.text: Nuclear charge, shielding and distance influence electron binding. Compare corresponding subshells rather than attributing every difference solely to electron count.

example.prompt: A simplified spectrum for one neutral atom shows three occupied subshell peaks, assigned 1s, 2s and 2p, with relative areas 2:2:3. Identify its electron count and outer configuration.
steps: Add the populations: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 electrons.
With a neutral atom, seven electrons imply seven protons, identifying nitrogen.
example.conclusion: The configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p³. The 1s electrons are more strongly bound than the outer n = 2 electrons.

misconception: A peak is not one electron or one individual orbital. A subshell peak may represent several electrons.
apTip: Use intensity and binding energy together, and state which attraction or shielding comparison supports an assignment.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.6; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Electron population gives Z=7 for the specified neutral atom. Core versus outer binding ordering checked; no axis-direction assumption or quantum calculation required.

title: Periodic Trends
overview: Periodic trends emerge from competition between attraction to the nucleus, shielding by other electrons and the distances of occupied energy levels. Use these mechanisms to explain comparisons rather than relying only on arrow diagrams.

keyConcepts.title: Across a period
keyConcepts.text: Increasing nuclear charge with broadly similar core shielding generally draws valence electrons closer. Atomic radius tends to decrease while first ionization energy generally increases.

keyConcepts.title: Down a group
keyConcepts.text: Additional principal levels place outer electrons farther from the nucleus and increase shielding. Atomic radius generally increases and first ionization energy generally decreases.

keyConcepts.title: Exceptions and ions
keyConcepts.text: Subshell energies and electron pairing can interrupt simple ionization-energy trends. Within an isoelectronic series, greater proton count generally produces a smaller radius.

example.prompt: Compare the radii of O²⁻, F⁻ and Na⁺. Their atomic numbers are 8, 9 and 11.
steps: Each ion has ten electrons: 8 + 2, 9 + 1 and 11 − 1.
Because their electron configurations match, compare nuclear attraction: eleven protons attract the same electron population more strongly than eight.
example.conclusion: The radius order is O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺. This comparison does not require assuming that all anions are larger than all cations.

misconception: More protons alone cannot explain every comparison across different principal energy levels; distance and shielding also matter.
apTip: Name the particles and explain the attractive force. A trend arrow without a mechanism is an incomplete justification.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.7; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Isoelectronic counts and proton ordering checked independently. Trend exceptions are acknowledged, avoiding an absolute monotonic claim.

title: Valence Electrons and Ionic Compounds
overview: Valence electrons largely govern main-group bonding and common ionic charges. Ionic formulas express charge-neutral ratios of cations and anions in an extended solid, rather than isolated molecules.

keyConcepts.title: Valence patterns
keyConcepts.text: Main-group atoms in the same group generally have similar outer electron configurations. These patterns help predict electron loss or gain in familiar ionic compounds.

keyConcepts.title: Charge balance
keyConcepts.text: Total positive and negative charge must cancel. Choose the smallest whole-number ratio of ions, keeping each ion’s identity and charge intact.

keyConcepts.title: Formula interpretation
keyConcepts.text: Subscripts count ions in a formula-unit ratio. Parentheses keep a polyatomic ion together when more than one copy is required.

example.prompt: Determine the formula for an ionic compound containing Mg²⁺ and N³⁻.
steps: Find the smallest shared charge magnitude: six. Three Mg²⁺ ions contribute +6, and two N³⁻ ions contribute −6.
The neutral ratio is therefore three magnesium ions to two nitride ions.
example.conclusion: The formula is Mg₃N₂. The subscripts describe ion ratios; they do not change Mg²⁺ into Mg³⁺ or N³⁻ into N²⁻.

misconception: Ionic charge is not a subscript to copy directly. A plausible-looking formula can still carry a net charge.
apTip: Check the signed charge sum after writing a formula. Use the formula-unit ratio when converting moles of compound into moles of a particular ion.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 1.8; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Charge products +6 and -6 cancel; 3:2 ratio is reduced. Main-group scope avoids unsupported transition-metal charge generalizations.

title: Types of Chemical Bonds
overview: Chemical bonding reflects electrostatic interactions among nuclei and electrons. Ionic, covalent and metallic models describe different arrangements of particles and electron density; real bonds can have intermediate character.

keyConcepts.title: Ionic model
keyConcepts.text: Cations and anions attract in an extended structure. Electron transfer is a useful account of ion formation, but the attraction between opposite charges holds the solid together.

keyConcepts.title: Covalent model
keyConcepts.text: Atoms share electron density. An electronegativity difference can make that sharing unequal, producing bond polarity without requiring complete electron transfer.

keyConcepts.title: Metallic model
keyConcepts.text: Positive metal cores are held together through attraction to delocalized valence electrons. Mobile electrons help explain electrical conductivity in metals.

example.prompt: Classify the dominant bonding models in solid NaCl, an isolated HCl molecule and solid Cu.
steps: NaCl contains an extended arrangement of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, so the ionic model applies.
HCl contains a shared electron pair attracted more strongly toward chlorine, giving a polar covalent bond.
example.conclusion: Cu is described by metal cores and delocalized electrons. Its bonding is not a collection of separate Cu₂ molecules.

misconception: A polar covalent bond is not automatically an ionic bond, and a numerical electronegativity cutoff is not a universal physical boundary.
apTip: Connect the particle arrangement and electron behavior to an observed property. Distinguish bond polarity from the overall polarity of a molecule.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 2.1; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Classifications checked for specified states and particle models; ionic attraction separated from transfer and bond polarity distinguished from molecular polarity.

title: Intramolecular Force and Potential Energy
overview: A bond’s potential-energy curve describes how energy changes as two atoms approach or separate. The stable bond distance occurs where competing attractions and repulsions produce a minimum in potential energy.

keyConcepts.title: Attractive region
keyConcepts.text: At moderate separation, attractions between electrons and the other nucleus can lower the system’s potential energy as atoms approach.

keyConcepts.title: Short-range repulsion
keyConcepts.text: At very short separation, nucleus–nucleus and electron–electron repulsions cause the energy to rise sharply. A shorter distance is therefore not always more stable.

keyConcepts.title: Bond length and strength
keyConcepts.text: The minimum identifies equilibrium bond length. Relative to separated atoms, a deeper well generally indicates more energy required to break that bond.

example.prompt: Two hypothetical bonds have minima at −300 and −450 kJ/mol relative to separated atoms at zero. Which requires more energy to dissociate?
steps: Breaking the first bond raises its potential energy by 300 kJ/mol.
Breaking the second raises it by 450 kJ/mol, requiring 150 kJ/mol more energy.
example.conclusion: The second bond is stronger by this measure. The well depths alone do not determine which bond has the shorter equilibrium distance; the horizontal positions are also needed.

misconception: The minimum is not a point where all electric interactions vanish. It represents a balance giving zero net force at equilibrium.
apTip: Read both axes and the chosen energy reference. Explain strength using energy differences and length using the location of the minimum.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 2.2; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Energy signs and changes independently checked. Depth does not alone establish length; net-force balance distinguished from absence of forces.

title: Structure of Ionic Solids
overview: An ionic solid is an extended arrangement of oppositely charged ions. Its macroscopic behavior follows from electrostatic attractions throughout the lattice and from whether charged particles can move.

keyConcepts.title: Lattice arrangement
keyConcepts.text: Each ion interacts with surrounding ions in three dimensions. A formula unit gives the simplest neutral ratio, not an individual molecule embedded in the crystal.

keyConcepts.title: Attraction strength
keyConcepts.text: For comparable arrangements, larger charge magnitudes and smaller ion separations generally strengthen electrostatic attraction. Compare both charge and size rather than only one variable.

keyConcepts.title: Properties
keyConcepts.text: Ions in an intact solid cannot move freely, so the solid usually does not conduct electricity. Molten salts and aqueous ionic solutions conduct when mobile ions are present.

example.prompt: Compare the expected electrostatic attractions in NaF and MgO, assuming broadly comparable ion separations.
steps: Na⁺ and F⁻ have charge magnitudes one; their charge product has magnitude one.
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have magnitudes two; their product has magnitude four.
example.conclusion: The larger charge product supports stronger attractions in MgO under the stated comparison. Exact lattice energies also depend on distances and crystal structure.

misconception: Strong lattice attractions do not imply that a solid conducts. Conductivity requires charge mobility, not merely charged particles.
apTip: Use a particle-level explanation for melting, brittleness or conductivity. Do not assume that every ionic solid dissolves readily in water.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 2.3; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Charge products checked independently; conditional distance/structure comparison avoids numerical lattice-energy claim or blanket solubility rule.

title: Structure of Metals and Alloys
overview: Metallic bonding involves metal cores attracted to delocalized valence electrons. Because the bonding is not restricted to fixed pairs of neighboring atoms, many metals can change shape while maintaining cohesion.

keyConcepts.title: Conductivity
keyConcepts.text: Mobile electrons carry charge through a metal. In an electrical circuit, the metal’s atoms need not travel from one end of the wire to the other.

keyConcepts.title: Malleability
keyConcepts.text: Layers of metal cores can shift while remaining attracted to the shared electron population. This differs from an ionic lattice, where displacement can bring like charges together.

keyConcepts.title: Alloy structures
keyConcepts.text: Substitutional alloys replace some metal atoms with similarly sized atoms. Interstitial alloys place sufficiently small atoms in spaces between larger metal atoms, often hindering layer motion.

example.prompt: A hypothetical alloy contains 90 g Cu and 10 g Zn. The Zn atoms replace some Cu atoms at lattice sites. Classify the alloy and find its zinc mass percentage.
steps: Replacement at metal lattice sites identifies a substitutional alloy.
The total mass is 100 g, so zinc contributes 10/100 × 100 = 10% by mass.
example.conclusion: The mass percentage does not mean 10% of the atoms are Zn; atom fraction would require converting each mass to moles.

misconception: An alloy is not necessarily a compound with a fixed formula. Its properties can change with composition and microscopic structure.
apTip: Connect the stated atomic sizes and positions to the alloy model, and distinguish mass fraction from particle fraction.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 2.4; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Substitutional criterion and composition checked; mass-to-atom distinction prevents an incorrect equal-fraction inference.

title: Lewis Diagrams
overview: Lewis diagrams account for valence electrons as bonding pairs and lone pairs. They are bookkeeping models that help predict connectivity and prepare for shape analysis, rather than literal drawings of electron trajectories.

keyConcepts.title: Count electrons
keyConcepts.text: Add valence electrons from each atom, adding electrons for a negative ionic charge or subtracting for a positive charge. Count the total before arranging bonds.

keyConcepts.title: Build the structure
keyConcepts.text: Choose a plausible skeleton, connect atoms, complete terminal valence shells and place remaining electrons. Hydrogen normally forms one bond; second-period central atoms follow the octet constraint.

keyConcepts.title: Check the result
keyConcepts.text: Every bonding pair and lone pair contributes to the total. Multiple bonds may be needed to satisfy octets, and ionic structures require brackets and an overall charge label.

example.prompt: Construct a Lewis description of CO₂. Carbon supplies four valence electrons and each oxygen supplies six.
steps: The available total is 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 electrons. Start with O–C–O connectivity.
Two C=O double bonds and two lone pairs on each oxygen use sixteen electrons and give every atom an octet.
example.conclusion: The resulting connectivity is O=C=O. A double bond contains four shared electrons, while each lone pair contains two.

misconception: A drawn line represents an electron pair, not one electron. A Lewis diagram alone is also not a complete three-dimensional shape description.
apTip: Recount electrons after adding multiple bonds, and check the total charge before applying a geometry model.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 2.5; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: 16-electron count checked; 8 bonding plus 8 nonbonding electrons satisfy three octets without exceeding carbon’s octet.

title: Resonance and Formal Charge
overview: Resonance represents electron delocalization when more than one valid Lewis arrangement describes the same connected atoms. Formal charge helps evaluate electron bookkeeping and compare candidate structures.

keyConcepts.title: Formal charge
keyConcepts.text: For an atom, formal charge equals valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons. Sum all atomic formal charges to recover the species’ overall charge.

keyConcepts.title: Resonance contributors
keyConcepts.text: Keep atomic connectivity fixed while rearranging electrons and bond locations. Equivalent contributors indicate a symmetric distribution, not separate molecules switching rapidly between drawings.

keyConcepts.title: Relative importance
keyConcepts.text: Structures with reasonable octets, reduced charge separation and favorable placement of negative formal charge often contribute more. Formal charges are not the same as measured partial charges.

example.prompt: In one nitrate-ion contributor, N is central with one N=O bond and two N–O bonds. Determine the formal charges.
steps: Nitrogen has no lone pairs and eight bonding electrons: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.
The double-bonded O has formal charge zero; each single-bonded O has −1. Their sum is +1 + 0 − 1 − 1 = −1.
example.conclusion: Three equivalent contributors place the double bond on different oxygens. Actual N–O bonding is delocalized, rather than one permanently distinct double bond.

misconception: Resonance moves electrons in a model, not atoms between different skeletons. The real ion is not any one contributor alone.
apTip: Check the charge sum and connectivity before comparing resonance drawings. Explain equivalent bonds using delocalization rather than rapid structural switching.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 2.6; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: N and O formal charges recomputed from valence ownership; total -1 and equivalent nitrate connectivity verified.

title: VSEPR and Hybridization
overview: VSEPR predicts three-dimensional arrangements by treating bonding regions and lone pairs as electron domains that repel. Molecular geometry describes atom positions, while electron-domain geometry includes lone pairs.

keyConcepts.title: Count domains
keyConcepts.text: Each single, double or triple bond counts as one region of electron density around the central atom. A lone pair counts as another domain.

keyConcepts.title: Geometry and polarity
keyConcepts.text: Use domain arrangement to identify molecular shape, then combine bond dipoles as vectors. Polar bonds can cancel in a symmetric molecule but need not cancel in an asymmetric one.

keyConcepts.title: Hybridization model
keyConcepts.text: Two, three and four domains correspond to the familiar sp, sp² and sp³ descriptions. Hybridization is a bonding model, not an extra electron-counting rule.

keyConcepts.title: Multiple bonds
keyConcepts.text: A double bond contains one σ and one π bond; a triple bond contains one σ and two π bonds.

example.prompt: Use NH₃ to connect its Lewis description, geometry and polarity.
steps: Nitrogen has three N–H bonds and one lone pair: four electron domains with a tetrahedral domain arrangement.
Considering only atom positions gives a trigonal-pyramidal molecular shape. The lone pair compresses the H–N–H angle below the ideal tetrahedral angle.
example.conclusion: The bond dipoles do not cancel, so NH₃ is polar; the common hybridization description for nitrogen is sp³.

misconception: Four electron domains do not always mean a tetrahedral molecular shape. Lone pairs affect the atom arrangement even though they are not drawn as bonded atoms.
apTip: Count domains from a valid Lewis structure, distinguish the two geometry labels and justify polarity using shape as well as bond polarity.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 2.7; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: NH3 electron-domain count, lone pair, pyramidal shape and noncanceling dipoles checked. Only sp/sp2/sp3 hybridization used; no d-orbital hybridization claim. Sigma/pi multiplicities verified for double and triple bonds.

title: Intermolecular and Interparticle Forces
overview: Interparticle attractions help explain boiling, melting and solution behavior. Identify the particles first: attractions between molecules differ from the covalent bonds that hold each molecule together.

keyConcepts.title: Dispersion
keyConcepts.text: Temporary fluctuations in electron density produce attractions in all atoms and molecules. Greater polarizability and effective contact can increase dispersion attractions.

keyConcepts.title: Permanent polarity
keyConcepts.text: Polar molecules can exhibit dipole–dipole attractions in addition to dispersion. Hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen bonded to N, O or F interacting with an appropriate lone pair.

keyConcepts.title: Ions in solution
keyConcepts.text: Ion–dipole attractions occur between ions and polar solvent molecules. Their strength depends on charge, distance and solvent orientation.

example.prompt: Compare the boiling behavior of ethanol and dimethyl ether, which share formula C₂H₆O.
steps: Both molecular substances exhibit dispersion and have polar bonds.
Ethanol has an O–H group and can form hydrogen-bonded networks among its own molecules; dimethyl ether lacks that donor group.
example.conclusion: Ethanol’s stronger overall intermolecular attractions help explain its higher boiling temperature, without claiming that its covalent bonds must break during boiling.

misconception: A molecule containing oxygen does not automatically hydrogen-bond to identical molecules. A suitable hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor arrangement matters.
apTip: Name the relevant attractions and connect them to the energy needed to separate particles. Do not claim that boiling necessarily breaks intramolecular bonds.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.1; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Isomer formulas, donor/acceptor distinction and phase-change mechanism checked. Ether can accept hydrogen bonds from water but is not its own conventional donor.

title: Properties of Solids
overview: Solid properties depend on the particles present and the interactions connecting them. Distinguish molecular, ionic, metallic and covalent-network solids before predicting conductivity, hardness or melting behavior.

keyConcepts.title: Molecular solids
keyConcepts.text: Discrete molecules are held together by intermolecular attractions. Melting typically overcomes these attractions while leaving the molecules’ internal covalent bonds intact.

keyConcepts.title: Extended structures
keyConcepts.text: Ionic solids contain ion lattices, metallic solids contain delocalized electrons, and covalent-network solids contain extended covalent bonding rather than separate small molecules.

keyConcepts.title: Property reasoning
keyConcepts.text: Strong attractions can increase melting temperature, but electrical conductivity requires mobile charge. Structure and mobility must both enter the explanation.

example.prompt: Explain why solid diamond and solid copper differ in electrical conductivity.
steps: Diamond’s atoms form a three-dimensional covalent network in which valence electrons are localized in bonds.
Copper’s metallic structure includes mobile delocalized electrons that can carry charge through the solid.
example.conclusion: Copper conducts readily, whereas pure diamond is a poor electrical conductor under ordinary conditions. The difference is not simply whether their bonds are strong.

misconception: All covalent substances do not have low melting points. A network solid can require breaking many covalent connections rather than separating discrete molecules.
apTip: Identify the structural category from particle evidence, then explain the specific observed property. Remember that different structures of the same element can behave differently.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.2; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Diamond versus copper charge mobility checked; network and molecular distinction retained, avoiding a universal rule for all carbon structures.

title: Solids, Liquids, and Gases
overview: Solids, liquids and gases differ in particle arrangement, spacing and freedom of motion. A change of state usually changes these relationships without changing the chemical identity of the particles.

keyConcepts.title: Solid
keyConcepts.text: Particles occupy relatively fixed positions while vibrating. Their arrangement may be ordered or disordered; being solid does not mean particles stop moving.

keyConcepts.title: Liquid
keyConcepts.text: Particles remain close together but can move past one another. A liquid has a relatively fixed volume while adopting the shape of its container.

keyConcepts.title: Gas
keyConcepts.text: Particles are widely separated relative to their sizes and move throughout the available space. Gas compressibility largely reflects the empty space between particles.

example.prompt: A sealed sample of liquid water evaporates into a larger available space. Describe its particles before and after vaporization.
steps: The particles remain H₂O molecules; their internal O–H bonds are not generally broken by this physical change.
Average separation increases greatly in the vapor, and molecules can move throughout the available volume.
example.conclusion: If vaporization occurs at constant temperature, added energy changes intermolecular potential energy rather than requiring a rise in average kinetic energy.

misconception: Particles do not grow larger when a substance expands. Increasing spacing can increase sample volume while individual molecular size remains essentially unchanged.
apTip: Distinguish particle size, spacing and motion in a diagram. Check whether the described process changes phase or produces new chemical species.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.3; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Physical vaporization and constant-temperature energy distinction checked; no claim of molecular enlargement or stationary solid particles.

title: Ideal Gas Law
overview: The ideal gas law relates pressure, volume, amount and absolute temperature for a simplified gas model. Consistent units and a clear distinction between fixed and changing quantities are essential.

keyConcepts.title: Equation
keyConcepts.text: PV = nRT uses temperature in kelvin. Select a gas constant whose pressure and volume units match the measurements, or convert the measurements first.

keyConcepts.title: Proportional reasoning
keyConcepts.text: At fixed n and T, pressure varies inversely with volume. At fixed n and V, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature, not Celsius temperature.

keyConcepts.title: Mixtures
keyConcepts.text: For ideal gases sharing a container, total pressure is the sum of partial pressures. Each partial pressure reflects that gas’s amount under the same volume and temperature.

example.prompt: An ideal sample contains 2.00 mol at 300 K in 24.6 L. Find pressure using R = 0.0820 L·atm/(mol·K).
steps: Rearrange to P = nRT/V. The numerator is 2.00(0.0820)(300) = 49.2 L·atm.
Divide by 24.6 L to obtain 2.00 atm.
example.conclusion: The liters cancel, leaving pressure units. Halving the volume at the same temperature and amount would double the pressure.

misconception: Doubling Celsius temperature does not generally double pressure. Convert to kelvin before using temperature ratios.
apTip: Write the units through the calculation and state which quantities remain fixed before applying a proportional relationship.

title: Kinetic Molecular Theory
overview: Kinetic molecular theory connects gas behavior to particles moving and colliding. The ideal model treats particles as negligibly small, with no intermolecular attractions and elastic collisions.

keyConcepts.title: Temperature and energy
keyConcepts.text: Average translational kinetic energy depends on absolute temperature. Different ideal gases at the same temperature have the same average translational kinetic energy.

keyConcepts.title: Mass and speed
keyConcepts.text: Equal average kinetic energy does not mean equal speed. Lighter particles have greater root-mean-square speed at the same temperature.

keyConcepts.title: Pressure
keyConcepts.text: Collisions with container walls transfer momentum and produce pressure. Changing particle number, speed or available volume affects collision behavior.

example.prompt: Compare the root-mean-square speeds of H₂ and O₂ at the same temperature, using molar masses 2.0 and 32.0 g/mol.
steps: Since vᵣₘₛ is proportional to 1/√M at fixed temperature, the ratio v(H₂)/v(O₂) is √(32/2).
The mass ratio is 16, so the speed ratio is 4.
example.conclusion: H₂ has four times the root-mean-square speed, but both samples still have the same average translational kinetic energy.

misconception: Gas particles do not all travel at the same speed. Temperature describes an average over a distribution, not the speed of every individual particle.
apTip: Check whether a comparison asks about speed, kinetic energy or pressure. State the fixed-temperature condition when using inverse-square-root mass reasoning.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.5; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: RMS ratio independently derived from equal average translational kinetic energy and mass ratio; energy and speed conclusions separated.

title: Deviation from Ideal Gas Law
overview: Real gases deviate from the ideal model because particles attract one another and occupy space. The dominant correction depends on conditions, so deviations can occur in more than one direction.

keyConcepts.title: Attractions
keyConcepts.text: At fixed amount, volume and temperature, attractions can reduce wall-collision momentum transfer and lower measured pressure relative to the ideal prediction.

keyConcepts.title: Finite particle volume
keyConcepts.text: At high density, the space occupied by particles becomes significant compared with container volume. Excluded-volume effects can raise pressure relative to a point-particle prediction.

keyConcepts.title: Conditions
keyConcepts.text: Low temperature makes attractions more influential relative to kinetic energy. Low density and sufficiently high temperature often make ideal behavior a better approximation.

example.prompt: At fixed n, V and T, a sample’s measured pressure is below nRT/V. Which nonideal effect is consistent with that direction?
steps: A pressure reduction is consistent with attractive interactions lowering the momentum transferred to the walls.
Finite-volume effects alone would tend to push pressure in the opposite direction under this comparison.
example.conclusion: The observation supports an attraction-dominated deviation; it does not mean particle volume is literally zero or attractions are the only interaction present.

misconception: Real gas pressure is not always lower than ideal pressure. Attractive and excluded-volume effects compete.
apTip: Identify what is held fixed, compare measured and ideal values, and explain the direction using the relevant particle-level assumption.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.6; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Fixed-state pressure comparison and competing correction directions checked; approximation conditions qualified rather than asserted universally.

title: Solutions and Mixtures
overview: A solution is a homogeneous mixture at the particle scale. Concentration specifies how much solute is present relative to a stated amount of solution or solvent, so the denominator must remain explicit.

keyConcepts.title: Molarity
keyConcepts.text: Molarity M equals moles of solute divided by liters of solution. It uses final solution volume, not automatically the volume of solvent initially added.

keyConcepts.title: Dilution
keyConcepts.text: Adding solvent lowers concentration while conserving solute amount, provided no reaction, loss or additional solute occurs. The relationship M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ follows from that mole balance.

keyConcepts.title: Species
keyConcepts.text: A molecular solute and a dissociating ionic solute can produce different numbers and identities of dissolved particles for the same formula-unit concentration.

example.prompt: Dilute 20.0 mL of 0.250 M NaCl to a final solution volume of 100.0 mL. Find the final formula-unit concentration.
steps: The initial solute amount is 0.250 mol/L × 0.0200 L = 0.00500 mol.
Divide by the final 0.1000 L to obtain 0.0500 M NaCl.
example.conclusion: Assuming complete dissociation, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ each have concentration 0.0500 M. Their combined ion concentration is 0.100 M.

misconception: Dilution does not remove solute. It changes the amount of solvent and the solution volume around the same conserved solute amount.
apTip: Convert volume to liters for mole calculations, and distinguish formula-unit concentration from concentrations of individual ions.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.7; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Mole conservation, final-volume denominator and 1:1 NaCl dissociation checked independently.

title: Representations of Solutions
overview: Particle representations connect a solution’s formula, composition and concentration to its microscopic contents. Read the key and the represented volume before interpreting the number or arrangement of symbols.

keyConcepts.title: Dissociation
keyConcepts.text: A soluble ionic compound may appear as separated ions rather than intact formula units. The ion ratio and total charge must match the chemical formula.

keyConcepts.title: Concentration
keyConcepts.text: For equal represented volumes, more solute particles indicate greater concentration. If diagram volumes differ, particle counts alone are insufficient.

keyConcepts.title: Solvation
keyConcepts.text: Water’s partially negative oxygen end tends to face cations, while its partially positive hydrogen ends tend to face anions. Solvation does not create covalent water–ion molecules.

example.prompt: Represent complete dissolution of three formula units of CaCl₂ in water.
steps: Each formula unit supplies one Ca²⁺ ion and two Cl⁻ ions, giving three calcium ions and six chloride ions.
Their total charges are +6 and −6, so the diagram remains electrically neutral.
example.conclusion: Show separated solvated ions rather than three permanently bonded CaCl₂ clusters. Water may be omitted only if the diagram clearly states that omission.

misconception: An ionic formula is a ratio, not evidence that dissolved ions must remain attached in fixed groups.
apTip: Check atom conservation, charge balance, solvent orientation and represented volume. Do not infer concentration from symbol size.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.8; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Ca:Cl count 3:6 and charge cancellation independently checked. Hydration orientation correct; formula units not treated as molecules.

title: Separation of Solutions and Mixtures
overview: Separation methods exploit physical differences between mixture components. Choose a method based on particle properties and interactions, not simply on whether the mixture looks uniform.

keyConcepts.title: Filtration
keyConcepts.text: A filter can retain an insoluble solid while liquid and dissolved solute pass through. Ordinary filtration does not separate dissolved salt ions from water.

keyConcepts.title: Chromatography
keyConcepts.text: Components partition differently between mobile and stationary phases. Stronger attraction to the stationary phase often produces less travel under otherwise comparable conditions.

keyConcepts.title: Volatility
keyConcepts.text: Distillation uses differences in vaporization behavior. The vapor can be enriched in a more volatile component, without requiring a chemical decomposition.

example.prompt: On the same paper chromatogram, a solvent front moves 8.0 cm and dye A moves 2.0 cm from the starting line. Find its retention factor.
steps: Measure both distances from the original baseline, not from the paper’s edge.
R_f = dye travel/solvent-front travel = 2.0/8.0 = 0.25.
example.conclusion: Compared with a dye traveling farther in this same setup, A is more strongly retained relative to the moving solvent. Different solvents or stationary phases can change the comparison.

misconception: An R_f value is not a universal identity independent of experimental conditions. A spot’s color alone also does not prove purity.
apTip: Explain separation using relative attractions or volatility, and identify which phase carries a component during the procedure.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.9; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Distance ratio and common baseline checked. Retention interpretation is relative to both phases and specified conditions, not an unconditional polarity ranking.

title: Solubility
overview: Dissolving involves separating some solute–solute and solvent–solvent contacts while forming solute–solvent interactions. Whether mixing is favorable depends on the overall balance, not just on a label such as polar or ionic.

keyConcepts.title: Compatible interactions
keyConcepts.text: Substances with similar dominant intermolecular interactions often mix well. “Like dissolves like” is a useful starting model, not an exception-free law.

keyConcepts.title: Ionic dissolution
keyConcepts.text: Water can stabilize separated ions through ion–dipole attractions. Strong lattice attractions can still limit an ionic solid’s solubility.

keyConcepts.title: Molecular structure
keyConcepts.text: Polar functional groups can interact with water, while a large nonpolar region may reduce favorable mixing. Compare the whole molecule rather than one atom alone.

example.prompt: Explain why ethanol mixes readily with water while a long-chain hydrocarbon does not mix extensively under ordinary conditions.
steps: Ethanol’s O–H group supports favorable hydrogen-bonding interactions with water.
A hydrocarbon offers mainly dispersion interactions and cannot replace water’s interaction network comparably.
example.conclusion: This particle-level comparison explains the observed contrast, but does not imply that every oxygen-containing compound is highly water-soluble.

misconception: All ionic compounds are not freely soluble, and dissolving does not necessarily release heat. Several energetic and dispersal contributions affect the outcome.
apTip: Identify interactions being disrupted and formed. Use a qualified explanation based on structure rather than treating polarity as a complete numerical solubility prediction.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.10; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Whole-molecule interaction reasoning checked; avoids blanket ionic solubility and exothermic-dissolution claims. No excluded colligative calculations.

title: Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
overview: Spectroscopy relates absorbed or emitted electromagnetic radiation to energy changes in matter. Different spectral regions often probe different kinds of molecular motion or electronic behavior.

keyConcepts.title: Radiation and energy
keyConcepts.text: Higher frequency corresponds to greater photon energy, while longer wavelength corresponds to lower frequency in the same propagation medium.

keyConcepts.title: Types of transitions
keyConcepts.text: Microwave absorption commonly probes molecular rotation, infrared probes vibration, and ultraviolet/visible radiation can produce electronic transitions. These are characteristic associations, not a guarantee that every molecule absorbs every wavelength.

keyConcepts.title: Spectral evidence
keyConcepts.text: Absorption occurs when radiation can drive an allowed transition with a matching energy gap. A spectrum’s pattern can provide structural evidence without being a direct photograph of a molecule.

example.prompt: A sample absorbs infrared radiation at a particular frequency. What type of energy change is most directly associated with that spectral region?
steps: Infrared absorption is associated with changes in molecular vibrational states.
The absorbed photon supplies the energy difference between the relevant states.
example.conclusion: This observation alone does not uniquely identify the sample or establish an electronic transition; additional spectral and chemical evidence is needed.

misconception: Absorbing radiation does not always break a bond. A transition can change a molecule’s energy state while its connectivity remains intact.
apTip: Match the spectral region to the type of transition, then distinguish what the observation supports from what it leaves uncertain.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.11; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Rotation/microwave, vibration/IR and electronic/UV-visible scope checked against CED; allowed-transition caveat avoids universal absorption claim.

title: Properties of Photons
overview: Photons carry discrete amounts of energy linked to frequency. For radiation in vacuum, c = λν and E = hν = hc/λ connect wavelength, frequency and energy per photon.

keyConcepts.title: Inverse wavelength relationship
keyConcepts.text: At fixed light speed, shorter wavelength means higher frequency and greater energy per photon. Convert wavelength into units compatible with c before calculating.

keyConcepts.title: Transitions
keyConcepts.text: Absorption increases an atom or molecule’s energy by the photon energy; emission decreases it by that amount. The relevant transition must match an available energy gap.

keyConcepts.title: Per photon versus per mole
keyConcepts.text: E = hν gives energy for one photon. Multiply by Avogadro’s constant only when a molar quantity is requested.

example.prompt: Find the energy of one 6.00 × 10² nm photon using c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
steps: Convert wavelength: 600 nm = 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m. Then ν = c/λ = 5.00 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹.
Multiply hν to obtain 3.313 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, approximately 3.31 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per photon.
example.conclusion: A shorter-wavelength photon would carry more energy, not less.

misconception: A larger wavelength does not mean a more energetic photon. Keep energy per photon separate from the total energy in a light pulse.
apTip: Cancel meters and seconds explicitly, and check that your final quantity answers the requested particle or molar scale.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.12; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Frequency and photon energy independently calculated; power-of-ten conversion from nanometers checked. Per-photon units not confused with molar energy.

title: Beer-Lambert Law
overview: The Beer–Lambert relationship connects absorbance with concentration for a suitable solution at a fixed wavelength. It supports quantitative analysis when the measurement conditions and linear range are controlled.

keyConcepts.title: Equation
keyConcepts.text: A = εbc, where ε is molar absorptivity, b is optical path length and c is concentration. Absorbance is dimensionless; the other units must cancel consistently.

keyConcepts.title: Proportionality
keyConcepts.text: For the same species, wavelength and path length within the linear range, absorbance is proportional to concentration. A calibration plot can determine an unknown concentration.

keyConcepts.title: Measurement conditions
keyConcepts.text: Use an appropriate blank and consistent cuvettes. Scattering, changing chemical speciation or excessive concentration can undermine a simple linear interpretation.

example.prompt: A solution has absorbance 0.300 in a 1.00 cm cell. Its molar absorptivity is 150 L/(mol·cm). Find concentration.
steps: Rearrange to c = A/(εb).
example.conclusion: Diluting to half that concentration would give absorbance 0.150 under the same conditions, provided the linear model still applies.

misconception: An absorbance of 0.300 does not mean 30.0% of light was absorbed. Absorbance is not a percentage scale.
apTip: Check the blank, wavelength, path length and calibration range before using a measured absorbance to infer concentration.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 3.13; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Units cancel to mol/L; inverse concentration calculation and half-concentration absorbance checked independently. Percent-absorption confusion explicitly avoided.

title: Introduction for Reactions
overview: A chemical reaction changes which substances are present by rearranging atoms and electrons. Connect a macroscopic observation to evidence about particle identity rather than treating any visible change as automatic proof of reaction.

keyConcepts.title: Evidence
keyConcepts.text: Gas formation, a precipitate, color change or energy transfer can support a reaction claim when interpreted in context. Each observation can also have physical explanations.

keyConcepts.title: Conservation
keyConcepts.text: A balanced equation conserves each element and total charge. It need not conserve the number of molecules because atoms can regroup into different particles.

keyConcepts.title: Representations
keyConcepts.text: Chemical formulas and state labels summarize reactants and products. Coefficients change amounts; changing a formula subscript changes the substance itself.

example.prompt: Interpret the balanced reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g).
steps: Two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule supply four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.
Two water molecules contain the same atom totals, but the atoms have different bonding partners.
example.conclusion: The number of molecules changes from three to two while every element is conserved. State labels specify vapor here; a different physical state would require its own label.

misconception: Balancing by changing H₂O to H₂O₂ would replace water with another substance rather than balance the intended reaction.
apTip: Check atom counts and charge separately. Explain why an observation supports new substance formation, and consider a plausible physical alternative.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.1; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Atom balance 4H/2O and molecule counts 3-to-2 checked independently. Observation inference qualified and product identity preserved.

title: Net Ionic Equations
overview: A net ionic equation displays the species that actually change in an aqueous reaction. Removing spectator ions makes the chemical process clearer without changing its atom or charge balance.

keyConcepts.title: Dissociation rules
keyConcepts.text: Separate dissolved strong electrolytes into ions in the complete ionic equation. Keep solids, liquids, gases and weak molecular species intact as appropriate.

keyConcepts.title: Spectators
keyConcepts.text: Ions appearing unchanged on both sides can cancel. Being present in a solution does not necessarily mean an ion participates in the reaction.

keyConcepts.title: Verification
keyConcepts.text: The remaining equation must conserve each element and total charge. Include state labels so the representation distinguishes dissolved ions from a precipitate.

example.prompt: Mix aqueous AgNO₃ and NaCl under conditions that produce solid AgCl. Write the net ionic equation.
steps: The complete ionic representation contains Ag⁺, NO₃⁻, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ on the reactant side, with AgCl(s), Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ as products.
Cancel the unchanged Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions.
example.conclusion: The net equation is Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Both sides contain one Ag and one Cl, and the total charge is zero.

misconception: Do not split the solid AgCl product into free aqueous ions; doing so would erase the precipitation process.
apTip: Identify electrolyte strength and physical state before canceling. A correctly balanced molecular equation does not automatically mean every written species belongs in the net ionic equation.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.2; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Spectators and state-specific splitting checked; atom and zero-net-charge balance verified for the precipitation reaction.

title: Representations of Reactions
overview: Particle diagrams represent reacting amounts through explicit counts of atoms, molecules or ions. Translate the key and reaction ratio before deciding what reacts, what remains and what the final diagram should contain.

keyConcepts.title: Conserved atoms
keyConcepts.text: Every atom in the initial diagram must appear somewhere in the final one for a closed system. Products can regroup atoms, but cannot create a missing element.

keyConcepts.title: Limiting reactant
keyConcepts.text: The limiting species runs out relative to the balanced stoichiometric ratio. The species with fewer drawn particles is not automatically limiting.

keyConcepts.title: Leftovers
keyConcepts.text: A final diagram can contain both products and unreacted excess reactant. Distinguish those particles instead of assuming everything disappears.

example.prompt: For the hypothetical reaction A₂ + 3B₂ → 2AB₃, begin with four A₂ molecules and nine B₂ molecules.
steps: Nine B₂ can react with three A₂, producing six AB₃ molecules.
One A₂ remains. The final counts are six AB₃, one A₂ and no B₂.
example.conclusion: Atom accounting confirms eight A atoms and eighteen B atoms both before and after the reaction.

misconception: Compare available reaction amounts using coefficients rather than choosing the smallest particle count. Here B₂ limits despite its larger initial count.
apTip: Redraw all remaining species and audit each element. A diagram must represent the same volume or amount basis if you compare concentrations.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.3; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Independent atom totals: initial A8/B18, final A6+2/B18. Reaction extent 9/3=3 yields six product molecules and one excess A2.

title: Physical and Chemical Changes
overview: Physical changes alter states, arrangements or distributions without necessarily forming new chemical substances. Chemical changes alter particle identities through changes in bonding or electron arrangement.

keyConcepts.title: Phase changes
keyConcepts.text: Melting and boiling usually change spacing and intermolecular relationships while preserving molecular identity. Individual particles do not have to break into atoms.

keyConcepts.title: Chemical transformations
keyConcepts.text: A reaction forms different chemical species, even if the total mass and element counts remain conserved. Macroscopic appearance alone may not identify those species.

keyConcepts.title: Evidence in context
keyConcepts.text: Reversibility, heat flow and bubbles are not exclusive tests for chemical change. Some reactions are reversible, while boiling produces bubbles without a new substance.

example.prompt: Compare boiling water with electrolyzing water into hydrogen and oxygen.
steps: Boiling produces H₂O vapor from H₂O liquid, so the molecule’s chemical identity is retained.
Electrolysis can be represented as 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, producing new substances with different bonding.
example.conclusion: Both processes involve energy and visible changes, but the second changes chemical identity. The balanced reaction still conserves hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

misconception: A change that is difficult to reverse is not automatically chemical, and a reversible change is not automatically physical.
apTip: Explain the distinction using named particles before and after, not only a list of observed signs. If identity is uncertain, state what additional evidence would help.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.4; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Phase versus decomposition species checked; electrolysis atom balance verified. Energy and reversibility are correctly treated as nonexclusive evidence.

title: Stoichiometry
overview: Stoichiometry uses a balanced equation to connect reacting and produced amounts. Convert to moles before applying coefficient ratios, and determine which reactant limits when more than one amount is supplied.

keyConcepts.title: Mole ratios
keyConcepts.text: Coefficients give ratios of particles or moles, not direct gram ratios. Mass conversions require the relevant molar masses.

keyConcepts.title: Limiting amount
keyConcepts.text: Compute the product possible from each reactant or compare moles divided by coefficients. The smaller allowed reaction extent controls theoretical yield.

keyConcepts.title: Yield and excess
keyConcepts.text: Theoretical yield follows from the limiting reactant. Actual yield is measured; excess reactant can remain even after a complete limiting-reactant consumption.

example.prompt: React 0.400 mol Al with 0.450 mol Cl₂ using 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. Find theoretical product and excess Al.
steps: The reaction extents are 0.400/2 = 0.200 and 0.450/3 = 0.150 mol of reaction, so Cl₂ limits.
Product is 2(0.150) = 0.300 mol AlCl₃. The same 0.300 mol of Al is consumed.
example.conclusion: Excess Al is 0.400 − 0.300 = 0.100 mol. The initial amounts cannot produce more product merely because some aluminum remains.

misconception: The smaller supplied mole amount is not always limiting; the balanced ratio determines how much is required.
apTip: Label every ratio with species and keep unrounded intermediate amounts until the final reported result.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.5; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Independent product-from-each-reactant comparison gives .400 versus .300 mol; chlorine limits and excess Al .100 confirmed.

title: Introduction to Titration
overview: A titration determines an unknown amount by reacting it with a measured amount of a solution of known concentration. The balanced equation connects the substances at equivalence.

keyConcepts.title: Mole accounting
keyConcepts.text: Convert titrant concentration and delivered volume into moles. Use the reaction’s stoichiometric ratio to determine analyte moles before dividing by sample volume.

keyConcepts.title: Equivalence and endpoint
keyConcepts.text: Equivalence is the stoichiometric completion condition. The endpoint is an observed signal, such as an indicator change, chosen to approximate that condition.

keyConcepts.title: Measurement
keyConcepts.text: Delivered buret volume is final reading minus initial reading. Use the original analyte sample volume when calculating its initial concentration.

example.prompt: A 20.0 mL H₂SO₄ sample requires 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH for complete neutralization. Find acid concentration.
steps: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O requires two moles of base per mole of acid.
NaOH amount is 0.100 × 0.0300 = 0.00300 mol; acid amount is 0.00150 mol.
example.conclusion: Divide by 0.0200 L to obtain 0.0750 M H₂SO₄. This is the concentration before adding titrant, not after dilution in the flask.

misconception: Equal titrant and analyte mole amounts are valid only for a 1:1 reaction. Equivalence also does not universally mean pH 7.
apTip: Balance first, distinguish endpoint from equivalence and check which solution the requested concentration describes.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.6; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Diprotic full-neutralization ratio, base moles and original acid-volume denominator independently verified; no unsupported pH inference.

title: Types of Chemical Reactions
overview: Reaction categories identify useful patterns in how species change. Precipitation, acid–base and oxidation–reduction descriptions emphasize different processes; one overall reaction can sometimes fit more than one description.

keyConcepts.title: Precipitation
keyConcepts.text: Dissolved ions combine into a poorly soluble solid. A net ionic equation shows the ions incorporated into that solid rather than the unchanged spectators.

keyConcepts.title: Acid–base
keyConcepts.text: A Brønsted acid donates a proton and a base accepts it. Neutralization can consume acid and base without requiring electron transfer between elements.

keyConcepts.title: Redox
keyConcepts.text: Oxidation numbers change as electrons are transferred or redistributed. Check oxidation states rather than assuming that any visible reaction must be redox.

example.prompt: Aqueous MgCl₂ and NaOH form Mg(OH)₂(s). Identify the primary reaction type.
steps: The net equation is Mg²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Mg(OH)₂(s).
Solid formation from dissolved ions identifies precipitation. Magnesium remains at oxidation number +2, and oxygen and hydrogen retain their usual states in hydroxide.
example.conclusion: This precipitation equation does not require a change in oxidation numbers. Sodium and chloride ions remain spectators in solution.

misconception: Forming a solid does not by itself show electron transfer. The equation and oxidation states supply the needed evidence.
apTip: Identify the changing species and name the process with a balanced equation. Allow overlapping descriptions when the actual chemistry supports them.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.7; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Precipitation state, charge balance and unchanged Mg/O/H oxidation numbers checked independently; no false universal exclusivity among categories.

title: Introduction to Acid-Base Reactions
overview: Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reactions transfer a proton between species. Identify the donor and acceptor in the actual equation rather than classifying a substance only from its formula.

keyConcepts.title: Acid and base
keyConcepts.text: An acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺. A base need not contain hydroxide before the reaction begins.

keyConcepts.title: Conjugate partners
keyConcepts.text: An acid and its conjugate base differ by one proton. The corresponding change in charge follows from gaining or losing H⁺.

keyConcepts.title: Water’s role
keyConcepts.text: Water can act as an acid or as a base depending on its reaction partner. Its behavior is contextual rather than permanently limited to one category.

example.prompt: Analyze NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻.
steps: NH₃ accepts a proton to become NH₄⁺, so NH₃ is the base and NH₄⁺ is its conjugate acid.
Water donates that proton to become OH⁻, making H₂O the acid and OH⁻ its conjugate base.
example.conclusion: Both atoms and charge balance: the neutral reactants produce charges +1 and −1 whose sum is zero.

misconception: Conjugate pairs are not simply any acid and base on opposite sides; they must differ by exactly one proton.
apTip: Trace the proton from donor to acceptor and identify both conjugate pairs. Do not assume that every acid–base mixture ends at neutral pH.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.8; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Proton transfer, conjugate identities and H/N/O plus charge balance checked; weak equilibrium arrow retained for ammonia in water.

title: Oxidation-Reduction (Redox) Reactions
overview: Oxidation–reduction reactions involve changes in oxidation numbers. Tracking those changes identifies which species loses electrons, which gains them and how electron transfer must balance.

keyConcepts.title: Oxidation numbers
keyConcepts.text: Use formal assignment rules to track electron ownership. An oxidation number is not necessarily an atom’s actual charge in a covalent molecule.

keyConcepts.title: Oxidation and reduction
keyConcepts.text: Oxidation increases oxidation number and corresponds to electron loss; reduction decreases it and corresponds to electron gain. The total electrons lost and gained must match.

keyConcepts.title: Agents
keyConcepts.text: The reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidized. The oxidizing agent accepts electrons and is reduced; the names describe their effects on the other species.

example.prompt: Analyze Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
steps: Zn changes from 0 to +2, losing two electrons. Cu changes from +2 to 0, gaining two electrons.
Half-reactions are Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Electrons cancel when added.
example.conclusion: Zn is the reducing agent; Cu²⁺ is the oxidizing agent. Total charge is +2 on each side of the overall equation.

misconception: The species being oxidized is the reducing agent, not the oxidizing agent. Keep the action and agent terminology distinct.
apTip: Assign oxidation numbers before naming agents, then verify electron count, element balance and total charge independently.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 4.9; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Half-reaction charges and two-electron cancellation checked; agent identities follow actual electron direction, not their product charges.

title: Reaction Rates
overview: Reaction rate measures how rapidly reactant or product amounts change. A concentration–time graph connects an average rate over an interval to an instantaneous rate given by a local slope.

keyConcepts.title: Sign and normalization
keyConcepts.text: Reactant concentration decreases, so its slope is negative. A positive reaction rate uses a minus sign and divides each species’ concentration change by its stoichiometric coefficient.

keyConcepts.title: Average versus instantaneous
keyConcepts.text: An interval quotient gives an average rate. A tangent slope gives an instantaneous rate, which can vary as the reaction proceeds.

keyConcepts.title: Units
keyConcepts.text: Concentration-based rates commonly use mol/(L·s), or M/s. The amount disappearing for one species need not equal the amount appearing for another.

example.prompt: For 2A → B, [A] falls from 0.800 M to 0.200 M over 10.0 s at constant volume. Find the average reaction rate.
steps: The A concentration slope is (0.200 − 0.800)/10.0 = −0.0600 M/s.
Divide its positive disappearance rate by two: reaction rate = 0.0300 M/s.
example.conclusion: B appears at 0.0300 M/s, half the magnitude of A’s disappearance rate, as required by the balanced ratio.

misconception: A reaction rate and a particular reactant’s disappearance rate are not always numerically identical. Check the coefficient convention.
apTip: Write the species and sign next to every slope, and distinguish an interval average from a rate at a single instant.

validation.reasoning: Concentration difference, interval quotient and stoichiometric half-factor independently checked under constant volume.

title: Introduction to Rate Law
overview: A rate law relates an observed reaction rate to reactant concentrations under specified conditions. Its exponents are determined from evidence and are not generally copied from the overall balanced equation.

keyConcepts.title: Experimental orders
keyConcepts.text: Compare experiments that change one concentration while holding the others and temperature fixed. A rate multiplier reveals the corresponding concentration exponent.

keyConcepts.title: Rate constant
keyConcepts.text: In rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, k contains the remaining proportionality and has units that depend on the total order m + n.

keyConcepts.title: Scope
keyConcepts.text: A zero order means the measured rate is independent of that concentration in the studied regime, not that the species is absent or irrelevant in every circumstance.

example.prompt: At constant temperature, doubling [A] quadruples rate, while doubling [B] at fixed [A] doubles rate. Determine the law.
steps: The A dependence is second order because 2² = 4; the B dependence is first order.
Thus rate = k[A]²[B], with total order three. If [A] = [B] = 0.100 M and rate = 0.00100 M/s, then k = 1.00 M⁻²s⁻¹.
example.conclusion: The units follow from dividing M/s by M³. The overall reaction coefficients alone could not establish this law.

misconception: A large coefficient in a balanced equation does not prove a high experimental order unless the step is explicitly elementary.
apTip: Choose comparisons that isolate one variable and verify the proposed law against every supplied experiment.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 5.2; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Exponent multipliers and rate constant .001/(.1²*.1)=1 independently checked; third-order constant units M^-2 s^-1 verified.

title: Concentration Changes Over Time
overview: Concentration–time data can identify reaction order by testing which transformed plot is linear. Use the correct slope relationship and rate-constant units for the proposed kinetic model.

keyConcepts.title: Linear plots
keyConcepts.text: For a single monitored reactant, zero order gives linear [A] versus time, first order gives linear ln[A], and second order gives linear 1/[A] under the corresponding rate laws.

keyConcepts.title: Slopes
keyConcepts.text: The zero- and first-order plots have slope −k; the second-order reciprocal plot has slope +k. Concentration falling over time does not by itself identify an order.

keyConcepts.title: First-order half-life
keyConcepts.text: A first-order half-life is constant and equals approximately 0.693/k. Equal time intervals remove equal fractions, rather than equal concentration amounts.

example.prompt: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0100 s⁻¹ and initial concentration 0.800 M. Find its half-life and concentration after two half-lives.
steps: The half-life is 0.693/0.0100 = 69.3 s.
After one half-life, concentration is 0.400 M; after two, it is 0.200 M.
example.conclusion: The two-half-life interval is 138.6 s. The second interval removes less absolute concentration but the same fraction as the first.

misconception: Constant half-life is a first-order property, not a universal property of every reaction.
apTip: Identify the plotted vertical variable before using a slope, and check the sign and units of k.
