validation.reasoning: Half-life quotient, repeated halving and total time independently checked. Integrated-plot scope matches zero/first/second-order CED relationships.

title: Elementary Reactions
overview: An elementary reaction is a single molecular event in a proposed mechanism. Its reactant stoichiometry can determine its mass-action rate expression, unlike the coefficients of an arbitrary overall multistep reaction.

keyConcepts.title: Molecularity
keyConcepts.text: Unimolecular and bimolecular steps involve one or two reacting particles in the elementary event. Simultaneous collisions among many particles are less probable.

keyConcepts.title: Rate expression
keyConcepts.text: For an explicitly elementary A + B → P step, the event rate is proportional to [A][B]. A step with two A particles gives a dependence on [A]².

keyConcepts.title: Overall versus step
keyConcepts.text: Adding elementary steps gives a net equation but generally does not give the overall experimental rate law by copying the summed coefficients.

example.prompt: An explicitly elementary step is A + B → AB. Predict how its rate changes when both reactant concentrations double at fixed temperature.
steps: The mass-action rate expression is k[A][B].
Doubling each factor multiplies rate by 2 × 2 = 4.
example.conclusion: If only [A] doubled while [B] stayed fixed, the multiplier would be two. The elementary-step assumption is essential to deriving the expression directly.

misconception: Writing a balanced overall equation does not establish that all its reactant particles collide in one elementary event.
apTip: Look for the word elementary or an explicit mechanism before inferring exponents from coefficients. State whether a rate refers to reaction events or a species’ consumption.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 5.4; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Bimolecular mass-action factors and fourfold scaling independently checked; no inference from unspecified overall coefficients.

title: Collision Model
overview: The collision model explains why particle contact alone is insufficient for reaction. A productive collision needs a suitable arrangement and enough energy to access the reaction pathway.

keyConcepts.title: Energy requirement
keyConcepts.text: Activation energy is a barrier along the pathway. Only a fraction of collisions have sufficient energy under the relevant model.

keyConcepts.title: Orientation
keyConcepts.text: Reacting sites must meet in a suitable geometry. Increasing collision frequency does not guarantee that every collision becomes productive.

keyConcepts.title: Temperature and concentration
keyConcepts.text: Higher temperature usually increases the fraction exceeding the barrier, while higher reactant concentration can increase collision opportunities. Distinguish these mechanisms.

example.prompt: Two samples have the same reactants and concentrations, but one is warmer. Explain a likely rate increase using collision theory.
steps: The warmer sample has a higher average kinetic energy and a changed distribution of collision energies.
A larger fraction can overcome the same activation barrier, increasing the frequency of successful collisions.
example.conclusion: This explanation does not require claiming that the activation energy itself falls when the sample is heated. The pathway may be unchanged.

misconception: Heating does not normally lower the activation barrier for an unchanged pathway. A catalyst changes the pathway rather than simply giving every particle more energy.
apTip: Connect a changed condition to collision frequency, orientation or energy distribution, and identify which factor the evidence actually changes.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 5.5; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Temperature distribution effect distinguished from barrier change; same-pathway and usual-rate qualifications prevent an absolute claim for every mechanism.

title: Reaction Energy Profile
overview: A reaction energy profile shows relative energies along a pathway. Separate the activation barrier from the overall reactant-to-product energy change: these answer different questions about kinetics and energetics.

keyConcepts.title: Barrier
keyConcepts.text: The forward activation barrier is the transition-state energy minus the reactant energy for that step. A higher barrier generally makes access less likely at the same temperature.

keyConcepts.title: Reaction energy
keyConcepts.text: The product energy minus reactant energy describes the net change. Products below reactants indicate energy release in the simplified profile.

keyConcepts.title: Reverse direction
keyConcepts.text: The reverse barrier is measured from the products to the same transition state, not from the reactants again.

example.prompt: A simplified profile assigns reactants 0, the transition state 80 and products −30 kJ/mol. Find the forward barrier, reverse barrier and net energy change.
steps: The forward barrier is 80 − 0 = 80 kJ/mol.
The reverse barrier is 80 − (−30) = 110 kJ/mol, and the net change is −30 − 0 = −30 kJ/mol.
example.conclusion: The reaction releases energy overall but still has a substantial forward barrier. Energy release alone does not establish a fast rate.

misconception: A downhill overall reaction is not barrier-free. Thermodynamic favorability and reaction speed are different properties.
apTip: Measure each barrier from the appropriate starting level and identify whether the diagram concerns one step or several.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 5.6; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Relative energy differences independently checked: 80 forward,110 reverse,-30 net. No rate inferred solely from downhill products.

title: Introduction to Reaction Mechanisms
overview: A reaction mechanism is a proposed sequence of elementary steps whose sum gives an overall reaction. Distinguish species that participate only along the pathway from those that remain in the net equation.

keyConcepts.title: Step addition
keyConcepts.text: Add reactants and products, then cancel identical species appearing on opposite sides. The remaining coefficients describe the overall stoichiometry.

keyConcepts.title: Intermediates
keyConcepts.text: An intermediate forms in one step and is consumed later. It can be absent initially and disappear from the net equation after cancellation.

keyConcepts.title: Evidence
keyConcepts.text: A mechanism must be consistent with stoichiometry and experimental kinetics, but agreement does not uniquely prove that no alternative pathway is possible.

example.prompt: Consider the hypothetical steps A + B → AB, followed by AB + B → AB₂. Find the net equation and intermediate.
steps: Adding the steps places AB on both sides, so it cancels.
The net result is A + 2B → AB₂. The AB species is formed then consumed, making it an intermediate.
example.conclusion: The summed equation conserves one A and two B atoms, but does not establish which step is slow or what experimental rate law is observed.

misconception: An intermediate is not automatically a catalyst. Its order of formation and consumption differs from that of a regenerated catalyst.
apTip: Check cancellation, atom and charge balance, then compare the proposed pathway with rate evidence rather than relying on the net equation alone.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 5.7; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Hypothetical molecular formulas preserve A1/B2 and intermediate cancellation; no unsupported claim that stoichiometry alone determines rate or verifies mechanism.

title: Reaction Mechanism and Rate Law
overview: A proposed mechanism connects elementary step rates to the observed rate law. A slow first step can provide a simple starting model, but intermediates require careful treatment when they occur in a rate expression.

keyConcepts.title: Slow-step model
keyConcepts.text: When a first elementary step controls the rate under the stated conditions, its reactant molecularity supplies the corresponding concentration dependence.

keyConcepts.title: Overall coefficients
keyConcepts.text: Stoichiometric coefficients in the net reaction need not match observed exponents because several elementary events can combine into that reaction.

keyConcepts.title: Consistency
keyConcepts.text: Compare the derived law with experimental concentration dependence. A matching law supports a mechanism but does not prove that it is the only possible one.

example.prompt: Suppose A + B → AB is slow, followed by fast AB + B → AB₂. Derive the predicted rate law.
steps: The stated rate-controlling first step is elementary and bimolecular, giving rate = k[A][B].
Adding the steps gives A + 2B → AB₂, but the second B enters after the controlling first event.
example.conclusion: The model therefore predicts first order in B, not second order merely because its net coefficient is two. Doubling B alone doubles the predicted rate.

misconception: Do not copy the final balanced equation into a rate law. Also, a later slow step containing an intermediate cannot always be expressed using initial reactants without another justified relationship.
apTip: Identify the elementary controlling step, state the kinetic assumptions and test the resulting concentration exponents against data.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 5.8; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Slow-first-step mass action and overall A1/B2 conservation independently checked; later-step intermediate caveat retained.

title: Pre-Equilibrium Approximation
overview: The pre-equilibrium approximation can remove an intermediate from a slow-step rate law when an earlier reversible step remains close to equilibrium. This is a kinetic assumption about the mechanism and conditions, not a rule for every multistep reaction.

keyConcepts.title: Fast reversible step
keyConcepts.text: For A + B ⇌ I, balancing forward and reverse step rates gives k₁[A][B] ≈ k₋₁[I].

keyConcepts.title: Substitution
keyConcepts.text: Solve for [I] ≈ (k₁/k₋₁)[A][B], then substitute into the slow-step rate expression. Keep the concentration factors and units.

keyConcepts.title: Validity
keyConcepts.text: The early equilibrium must be maintained sufficiently closely while the slower pathway proceeds. A fast reaction label alone does not justify every equilibrium substitution.

example.prompt: After that fast equilibrium, suppose I + B → P is slow with rate k₂[I][B]. Derive a reactant-only rate law.
steps: Substituting the equilibrium expression gives rate ≈ k₂(k₁/k₋₁)[A][B]².
example.conclusion: The predicted rate is 3(0.0400)(0.200) = 0.0240 M/s, matching the substituted expression.

misconception: An intermediate should not simply be deleted from a rate expression; a justified relationship is needed to replace its concentration.
apTip: Show the reversible-step relation explicitly before substitution, and distinguish this approximation from assuming the entire reaction has reached equilibrium.

validation.scope: Original review of canonical chemistry Topic 5.9; curriculum scope checked against the official CED. No copied lesson or exam material.
validation.reasoning: Forward/reverse balance and substitution independently recomputed; ratio units M^-1 and final M/s verified. No unsupported steady-state derivation.

title: Multistep Reaction Energy Profile
overview: A multistep reaction profile contains several transition-state peaks and intermediate valleys. Each step’s activation barrier must be measured from its own starting level, not from one common baseline.

keyConcepts.title: Peaks and valleys
keyConcepts.text: A peak represents a transition state. A valley between steps can represent an intermediate; neither is automatically a stable final product.

keyConcepts.title: Local barriers
keyConcepts.text: For each forward step, subtract the preceding minimum from that step’s peak. The highest absolute peak is not always the largest local barrier.

keyConcepts.title: Overall change
keyConcepts.text: The final product-to-initial-reactant difference gives the overall energy change. A catalyst or altered pathway can change barriers without changing those endpoint energies.

example.prompt: A hypothetical profile has reactants at 0, first peak at 80, intermediate at 50, second peak at 100 and products at −20 kJ/mol.
steps: The first barrier is 80 − 0 = 80 kJ/mol.
The second is 100 − 50 = 50 kJ/mol, despite its higher absolute peak. The overall change is −20 kJ/mol.
example.conclusion: If other kinetic factors are comparable, the larger first barrier can indicate a slower first step. The diagram alone does not uniquely establish an experimental rate law.

misconception: Do not choose a rate-controlling step simply by locating the highest point on the page. Starting levels and other kinetic factors matter.
apTip: Label all minima and peaks before calculating, then distinguish local barriers from the overall energy change.

validation.reasoning: Local energy subtraction 80 and 50 and overall -20 independently checked; kinetic conclusion qualified by other factors.

title: Catalysis
overview: A catalyst increases reaction rate by providing a different pathway and is regenerated over the catalytic cycle. Its role changes how quickly a system approaches equilibrium, not the equilibrium position at a fixed temperature.

keyConcepts.title: Pathway
keyConcepts.text: A catalytic route can lower an effective activation barrier or improve how reactants encounter one another. It does not need to increase the average kinetic energy of the sample.

keyConcepts.title: Regeneration
keyConcepts.text: A catalyst may be consumed in one step and produced in another, so it cancels from the net equation. An intermediate forms and is consumed within the pathway instead.

keyConcepts.title: Equilibrium
keyConcepts.text: Catalysts accelerate access in both directions without changing the reaction’s equilibrium constant or overall endpoint energy difference at the same temperature.

example.prompt: Consider the hypothetical steps A + C → AC and AC + B → AB + C. Identify the catalyst and intermediate.
steps: Adding the steps cancels C and AC, leaving A + B → AB.
C is consumed then regenerated, so it is the catalyst. AC forms then is consumed, so it is an intermediate.
example.conclusion: The cycle illustrates regeneration but does not by itself prove that this proposed pathway is faster; energy or kinetic evidence would support that claim.

misconception: A catalyst does not increase equilibrium yield merely by being present. It can help equilibrium be reached sooner.
apTip: Trace the species across all steps and distinguish evidence for a catalytic cycle from evidence for its actual rate enhancement.
